messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Product Manager
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rajesh's Vigil

Rajesh Mehta was thirty-two years old when the security forces came to his office in Karachi. He had been working as a junior accountant at a mid-sized textile firm, a job his parents had helped him secure through a family connection. It was 2001, and the political climate in the city had grown volatile. He had said nothing publicly, signed no petitions, attended no rallies. He was careful, or so he believed. But someone had named him—whether as an informant, a sympathizer, or simply a case of mistaken identity, he never learned.

They arrived in the late afternoon. Three men in civilian clothes, though one wore the unmistakable boots of the Rangers. They did not announce themselves. They pulled him from his desk and into a van. What followed over the next four days was systematic and deliberate. They kept him in a room with no windows. They used a generator that filled the space with incomprehensible noise—voices shouting in Urdu mixed with the mechanical roar, so loud and chaotic that he could not distinguish individual words, could not understand what was being said or what was being demanded. The confusion itself became a weapon. They applied electric current to his feet and genitals. They held his head underwater. They kept him awake for sixty hours. When they finally released him—no charges, no explanation—he could barely walk.

Now, at fifty-eight, twenty-three years later, Rajesh lived in New Jersey with his wife Priya, whom he had married three years after his release. They had two adult children. He had rebuilt a career, eventually reaching Product Manager at a software company. On the surface, he had moved forward. But the past had never truly released him.

The incomprehensible chatter of a crowded coffee shop could send him into a state of vigilant dread. The sound of sirens—whether from an ambulance or police car—would cause his chest to tighten and his hands to shake. Dizziness would come without warning, a sensation of the ground tilting beneath him, and he had learned to attribute it to the threat his body was always detecting. He had come to believe, with a certainty he could not shake, that the chaos and violence he had endured had marked him in some essential way—that there was something about him, something he carried, that had made him a target then and would make him vulnerable again. People could not be trusted. He had seen how easily ordinary men could become instruments of cruelty.

Over the years, he had constructed a life of careful avoidance. He did not drive past police stations. He took routes that avoided highways where he might encounter sirens. He had declined promotions that would require him to attend large conferences or travel internationally. At work, he had become known as the person who worked alone, who declined team lunches, who seemed perpetually stressed about something no one could identify. His colleagues attributed it to personality; they did not know that Rajesh was managing a constant internal inventory of danger.

At home, Priya had learned not to touch him suddenly. He would startle violently, his body flooding with adrenaline, and the shame of his reaction would linger for hours. She had stopped trying to comfort him in the ways a wife should be able to comfort a husband. He woke most nights at 2 or 3 a.m., his mind alert, checking the locks on the doors and windows, listening to the ambient sounds of the neighborhood, ensuring that nothing had changed, that no one had entered. He could not relax even on vacation, even in the safety of his own home, because relaxation felt like lowering his guard, and lowering his guard felt like inviting catastrophe.

His body had become a constant source of surveillance. He monitored his heart rate, his breathing, the tension in his muscles. Any irregularity—a skipped beat, a slight dizziness—was interpreted as a sign that danger was imminent, that his body knew something his conscious mind had not yet registered. He had seen three cardiologists in the past decade. All had told him his heart was healthy. He did not believe them.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment of clarity that came with unexpected pain. His daughter had called him on a Tuesday morning to tell him she was getting married. He should have felt joy. Instead, he felt a crushing certainty that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that his presence would somehow poison her happiness, that the universe had already decided his quota of suffering and his daughter would pay the price for being his child. The thought terrified him—not because it made rational sense, but because it felt absolutely true. That night, he told Priya he needed to see someone. He was afraid of what he might become if he did not.
